text: Himachal Pradesh, known in Hindi as Himācal Pradeś and literally meaning "snow-laden mountain province," is a mountainous state in northern India, situated in the Western Himalayas between 30°22′N and 33°12′N latitude and 75°47′E and 79°04′E longitude, covering an area of 55,673 square kilometres. It is the northernmost state of India and shares borders with Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh to the north, Punjab to the west, Haryana to the southwest, Uttarakhand to the southeast, and a narrow border with Uttar Pradesh to the south, while also having an international border with the Tibet Autonomous Region in China. The state is characterized by extreme landscapes, including several peaks and extensive river systems, with the Zanskar range in the northeast, the great Himalayan range in the east and north, the Dhauladhar and Pir Panjal ranges in the lesser Himalayas, and the Shiwalik range in the south and west. Reo Purgyil, at 6,816 metres, is the highest peak in the state. The drainage system includes perennial rivers such as the Chandra Bhaga (Chenab), Ravi, Beas, Sutlej, and Yamuna, which are fed by snow and rainfall and flow through valleys like the Satluj, Spiti, Baspa, Kullu, Kangra, Parvati, Lahaul and Pangi, and Chamba. These rivers contribute to both the Indus and Ganges basins. Due to elevation variations, the climate ranges from hot and humid in the south to cold, alpine, and glacial in the north and east; Dharamsala receives heavy rainfall, while Lahaul and Spiti are cold and nearly rainless. The state experiences three seasons: summer (mid-April to end of June), winter (late November to mid-March), and the rainy season. Himachal Pradesh is recognized as India's second open-defecation-free state in 2016 and was ranked as India's least corrupt state in a 2017 CMS-India Corruption Study. The state is divided into 12 districts, grouped into three divisions—Shimla, Kangra, and Mandi—and further subdivided into 73 subdivisions, 78 blocks, and 172 tehsils. It is one of the states in the Indian Himalayan Region (IHR), a global hotspot of biodiversity, with 463 bird, 77 mammalian, 44 reptile, and 80 fish species; the state bird is the Western tragopan (jujurana), and the state animal is the snow leopard. The state has five national parks—Great Himalayan National Park (a UNESCO World Heritage Site), Pin Valley, Inderkilla, Khirganga, and Simbalbara—and 30 wildlife sanctuaries and 3 conservation reserves. Himachal Pradesh is also known as Dev Bhoomi ("Land of Gods") and Veer Bhoomi ("Land of the Brave"). The region has been inhabited since prehistoric times by tribes such as the Koli, Hali, Dagi, Dhaugri, Dasa, Khasa, Kanaura, and Kirata, with the Kols and Mundas believed to be the original inhabitants, followed by the Bhotas and Kiratas. The foothills were inhabited by people from the Indus Valley Civilisation (2250–1750 BCE). During the Vedic period, small republics (Janapada) existed, later conquered by the Gupta Empire, and later fragmented into local powers including Rajput principalities, which were invaded by the Delhi Sultanate, Mahmud Ghaznavi, Timur, and Sikander Lodi. Several hill states acknowledged Mughal suzerainty. The Kingdom of Gorkha conquered territories in Nepal in 1768, expanded its territory, and annexed Sirmour and Shimla, defeating Kangra's ruler Sansar Chand Katoch in 1806, though they failed to capture Kangra Fort, which came under Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1809. After the First Anglo-Sikh War, Raja Ram Singh captured the Siba fort in 1846. The British came into direct conflict with the Nepali forces in the tarai belt, expelled them from the Satluj provinces, and emerged as the paramount power. During the 1857 revolt, hill states were largely inactive, except for some rulers like those of Chamba, Bilaspur, Bhagal, and Dhami, who supported the British. After Queen Victoria's proclamation in 1858, the British Crown took control. During World War I, rulers of Kangra, Jaswan, Datarpur, Guler, Rajgarh, Nurpur, Chamba, Suket, Mandi, and Bilaspur remained loyal and contributed to the war effort. On 15 April 1948, the Chief Commissioner's Province of Himachal Pradesh was established by integrating 30 princely states, including the Simla Hills States and four southern hill states of Punjab, under the Himachal Pradesh (Administration) Order, 1948. Bilaspur was merged into Himachal Pradesh on 1 July 1954 via the Himachal Pradesh and Bilaspur (New State) Act, 1954. Himachal became a Part 'C' state on 26 January 1950 and had its first Legislative Assembly election in 1952. On 1 November 1956, it became a union territory. On 1 November 1966, areas from Punjab—Simla, Kangra, Kullu, Lahul and Spiti, Lohara, Amb, Una Kanungo, Santokhgarh Kanungo, parts of Dhar Kalan Kanungo, and some parts of PEPSU and Pathankot—were merged into Himachal Pradesh under the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966. On 18 December 1970, the Himachal Pradesh Act was passed, and the state came into being on 25 January 1971 as the 18th state of India, with Dr. Yashwant Singh Parmar as its first chief minister. The state operates under a parliamentary system with a unicameral Legislative Assembly of 68 Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLA), with terms lasting five years. The executive authority lies with the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister, who is appointed by the Governor, the titular head of state appointed by the President of India. The Speaker and Deputy Speaker are elected by the members and preside over assembly meetings. The judiciary includes the Himachal Pradesh High Court and lower courts. Planning began in 1951, with the First Five-Year Plan allocating ₹52.7 million, of which over 50% went to transport and communication and 4.6% to power (rising to 7% by the Third Plan). Expenditure on agriculture increased from 14.4% in the First Plan to 32% in the Third Plan, declining to less than 10% by the Tenth Plan, while energy expenditure reached 24.2% in the Tenth Plan. The total GDP for 2005–06 was ₹254 billion, up from ₹230 billion in 2004–05, showing a 10.5% increase. In the November 2022 assembly elections, the Indian National Congress won 40 seats, the BJP won 25, and Sukhvinder Singh Sukhu was sworn in as the 15th Chief Minister on 11 December 2022, with Mukesh Agnihotri as deputy. The state government promotes sustainable development through its "Green Himachal vision," as highlighted by Town and Country Planning Minister Rajesh Dharmani in a statement on 29 March 2025. In 2002, a workshop on endangered medicinal plant species was held, attended by 40 experts, due to large-scale irrational extraction threatening biodiversity. According to the 2003 Forest Survey of India report, 66.52% of the state's area is legally defined forest. The state is known as the "fruit bowl of the country" with widespread orchards and cultivated flowers like white gladiolas, carnations, marigolds, roses, chrysanthemums, tulips, and lilies. The Himachal Pradesh Horticultural Produce Marketing and Processing Corporation Ltd. (HPMC) markets fresh and processed fruits. The state is also the first smoke-free state in India, with cooking free of traditional chulhas.

Planning in Himachal Pradesh began in 1951 alongside the rest of India with the implementation of the first five-year plan, which allocated ₹52.7 million to the state. More than 50% of this expenditure was directed toward transport and communication, while the power sector received only 4.6%, increasing to 7% by the Third Plan. Expenditure on agriculture and allied activities rose from 14.4% in the First Plan to 32% in the Third Plan, declining progressively to less than 10% by the Tenth Plan. Energy sector expenditure reached 24.2% in the Tenth Plan. The total GDP for 2005–06 was ₹254 billion, up from ₹230 billion in 2004–05, reflecting a 10.5% increase. In fiscal 2015–16, GDP was estimated at ₹1.110 trillion, rising to ₹1.247 trillion in 2016–17, a 6.8% growth, with per capita income increasing from ₹130,067 to ₹147,277. Fiscal 2017–18 advance estimates showed GDP at ₹1.359 trillion and per capita income at ₹158,462. As of 2018, Himachal Pradesh is the 22nd-largest state economy in India with a GDP of ₹1.52 lakh crore (US$18 billion) and the 13th-highest per capita income (₹160,000 or US$1,900). It ranks second in the country on human development indicators after Kerala. Under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (NREGA), Himachal Pradesh recorded a 46% share of workdays for women in 2009–2010, a sharp rise from 13% in 2006–2007. Agriculture contributes 9.4% to the net state domestic product and is the main source of income and employment, directly supporting 90% of the population and providing direct employment to 62% of total workers. Major crops include wheat, maize, rice, and barley, with cropping systems such as maize-wheat, rice-wheat, and maize-potato-wheat; pulses, fruits, vegetables, and oilseeds are also grown. The traditional Kuhl irrigation system is prevalent in the Kangra valley, though it faces threats from hydroprojects on small streams. Initiatives like the Mid-Himalayan Watershed Development Project and the Himachal Pradesh Reforestation Project (HPRP), the world’s largest clean development mechanism (CDM) undertaking, have improved agricultural yields and rural incomes. Apple is the principal cash crop, grown in Shimla, Kinnaur, Kullu, Mandi, Chamba, Sirmaur, and Lahaul-Spiti, with an average annual production of five lakh tonnes and per hectare output of 8 to 10 tonnes. Apple cultivation covers 49% of the area under fruit crops and 85% of total fruit production, generating an estimated economy of ₹3500 crore. Apple production increased from 90,347 hectares in 2000–01 to 104,000 hectares in 2011–12, and in fiscal 2015–16, it reached 753,000 tonnes, making Himachal the second-largest apple-producing state after Jammu and Kashmir. The state is also a leading producer of apricots, cherries, peaches, pears, plums, and strawberries. Kangra tea, introduced in 1849 and popular globally, peaked in the late 19th century, declined after the 1905 Kangra earthquake, and received geographical indication status in 2005. Himachal is known as Asia’s pharmaceutical hub, housing 652 pharmaceutical units and a thriving ₹40,000 crore drug manufacturing industry. Hydropower is a major source of income, with abundant perennial rivers supporting high-capacity plants that produce surplus electricity sold to states like Delhi, Punjab, and West Bengal. This electricity export revenue is used as a subsidy for state consumers. The state is nearly universally electrified, with 94.8% of houses receiving electricity as of 2001 (above the national average of 55.9%), though its hydroelectric potential of 27,436 MW across five river basins remains underutilized, with a capacity of 10,351 MW in 2016. Tourism is a major economic contributor, with hill stations like Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala, Dalhousie, Chamba, Khajjiar, Kullu, and Kasauli attracting domestic and foreign tourists. The state has five Shakti Peeths—Chintpurni, Jwalamukhi, Bajreshwari Mata, Shri Chamunda Devi, and Naina Devi—and prominent pilgrimage sites such as Baijnath, Bhimakali, Bijli Mahadev, and Jakhoo. Manimahesh Lake in Chamba hosts an annual August pilgrimage attracting lakhs of devotees. The state is referred to as "Dev Bhoomi" due to its presence in ancient Hindu texts and numerous historical temples. Adventure tourism includes ice skating in Shimla, paragliding in Bir and Solang Valley, rafting in Kullu, skiing in Manali, boating in Bilaspur, fishing in Tirthan Valley, trekking, and horse riding. Shimla hosts Asia’s only natural ice-skating rink. The state has some of the highest mountain passes in the world—Rohtang Pass, Baralacha La, Kunzum La, Borasu Pass, and Hamta Pass—and Spiti Valley, at over 3000 meters, is a popular destination with ancient Buddhist monasteries. Himachal hosted the first Paragliding World Cup in India from 24 to 31 October 2015 in Bir Billing, located 70 km from Mcleod Ganj in Kangra district, which is known as the launching site and considered the best for paragliding, with the landing site being Bir. The village also hosts cultural events like the Bir Music Festival. Over 2000 villages celebrate festivals such as Kullu Dussehra, Chamba’s Minjar, Renuka ji Fair, Lohri, Halda, Phagli, Losar, and Mandi Shivratri. There are approximately 6000 temples, including Bijli Mahadev, a 20-meter stone structure believed to attract lightning as a sign of divine blessings. The Great Himalayan National Park in Kullu, covering 620 km² from 1500 to 4500 meters, was established in 1984 and includes forest types like Deodar, Himalayan Fir, Spruce, Oak, and Alpine pastures, housing animals such as snow leopard, yak, Himalayan black bear, Western tragopan, monal, and musk deer. Sanctuaries like Naina Devi and Gobind Sagar (220 km²) in Una and Bilaspur host animals such as Indian porcupine and giant flying squirrel, with fish species including Mrigal, Silver carp, Katla, Mahaseer, and Rohu in Gobind Sagar Lake. Narkanda, located at around 8850 feet between the Giri and Sutlej river valleys, is known for its apple orchards. The state has three domestic airports in Kangra, Kullu, and Shimla districts, connecting it to New Delhi and Chandigarh. The only broad-gauge railway line runs from Amb Andaura–Una to Nangal Dam in Punjab and extends to Daulatpur, electrified since 1999, with a small section crossing into Himachal from the Pathankot–Jalandhar line. Himachal is known for narrow-gauge railways: the Kalka-Shimla Railway (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) and the Kangra Valley Railway, totaling 259 km; the operational railway network spans 296.26 km. Roads are the primary mode of transport due to the hilly terrain, with a total network of 28,208 km, including eight National Highways (1,234 km) and 19 State Highways (1,625 km). Hamirpur has the highest road density in the country. Some roads close during winter and monsoon due to snow and landslides. The state-owned Himachal Road Transport Corporation operates over 3,100 buses, and around 5,000 private buses serve the state. The 2011 Census recorded a total population of 6,864,602 (3,481,873 males, 3,382,729 females), representing 0.57% of India’s population with a 12.81% growth rate. The child sex ratio improved from 896 in 2001 to 909 in 2011. The total fertility rate (TFR) in 2015 was 1.7, one of the lowest in India. The state ranks 21st in population, followed by Tripura at 22nd, with Kangra District having the highest population at 1,507,223. Life expectancy increased from 52.6 years (1970–1975) to 72.0 years (2011–15), above the national average. The infant mortality rate was 40 in 2010, the crude birth rate declined from 37.3 in 1971 to 16.9 in 2010 (below the national average of 26.5 in 1998), and the crude death rate was 6.9 in 2010. The literacy rate nearly doubled between 1981 and 2011, reaching 83.78% in 2011. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes account for 25.19% and 5.71% of the population, respectively. The sex ratio is 972 females per 1,000 males, up from 968 in 2001. Main caste groups include Brahmins, Rajputs, Kanets, Gurjars, Kulindas, Ghirths, Kolis, Hollis, Chamars, Rehars, Lohars, Baris, Julahas, Turis, Batwals, and Dalits. Caste-based discrimination persists, especially affecting Dalit communities in rural areas, with recent incidents such as a 12-year-old Scheduled Caste boy’s suicide in Limbra village (17 September 2025) after being locked in a cowshed and harassed for allegedly entering an upper-caste woman’s house, leading to arrests under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Research shows upper castes hold fertile land, while depressed castes have less fertile land, and both major political parties rely on upper-caste votes. Hindi is the de jure official language, spoken as a lingua franca, with Sanskrit as the additional official language, encouraged for wider study and use. Most residents natively speak Western Pahari languages (locally called Himachali or Pahari), including Pahari (Mahasu Pahari, Pahari Kinnauri), Kangri, Mandeali, Bilaspuri, Chambeali, and Kullu.

The Prevention of Atrocities Act is referenced in the context of social dynamics in Himachal Pradesh, where fieldwork indicates that upper castes, particularly the Thakurs, hold predominantly fertile land, while depressed castes have limited access to land, which is often unfertile. Both major political parties in the state allocate election tickets and mobilize voters based on caste, with a clear dependence on Thakur or upper-caste support. Hindi is the de jure official language and serves as the majority lingua franca, with Sanskrit recognized as an additional official language, though it is primarily used in academic and symbolic settings. The majority of the population speaks Western Pahari languages—such as Kangri, Mandeali, Kullui, Bilaspuri, Chambeali, Gaddi, Sirmauri, Churahi, Hinduri, Pangwali, and Bhattiyali—locally known as Himachali or Pahari. Other spoken languages include Hindi (15.68%), Punjabi (4.42%), Nepali (1.30%), and Kinnauri (1.20%). Smaller communities speak Haryanavi (0.32%), Gujari (0.21%), Lahuli–Spiti (0.16%), Pattani (0.12%), Tibetan (0.3%), and various Kinnauri and Himalayan dialects such as Bhoti Kinnauri, Chitkuli Kinnauri, Bunan (or Gahri), Jangshung, Kanashi, Shumcho, Spiti Bhoti, Sunam, Tinani, Tukpa, Chinali, and Lahul Lohar. Hinduism is the dominant religion, with over 95% of the population adhering to it, primarily through Shaivism and Shaktism, which are evenly distributed across the state—Himachal Pradesh has the highest proportion of Hindus among all Indian states and union territories. Muslims are concentrated in Sirmaur, Chamba, Una, and Solan districts, making up 2.5–6.3% of the population, while Sikhs constitute 1.16% and are mainly urban; Buddhists account for 1.15%, forming a majority (62%) in Lahaul and Spiti and 21.5% in Kinnaur. The state remained largely untouched by external customs due to its difficult terrain, and has undergone rapid economic and social transformation. Culturally, Himachal is divided into three regions: Upper Himachal (Mahasu), Lower Himachal (Kangra, Hamirpur, Bilaspur, Una, and parts of Chamba), and the Lahaul and Spiti and upper Kinnaur districts. It is a multilingual state with Western Pahari languages widely spoken, including Kangri, Mandeali, Kullui, Chambeali, Bharmauri, and Kinnauri. Himachal is renowned for its handicrafts such as carpets, leather works, Kullu shawls, Kangra paintings, Chamba Rumals, stoles, embroidered grass footwear (Pullan chappal), silver jewellery, metal ware, knitted woolen socks, Pattoo, basketry (cane and bamboo), and woodwork, with growing domestic and international demand. Himachali caps, known for their color bands, symbolize political identity—Congress leaders like Virbhadra Singh wore green-banded caps, while BJP leader Prem Kumar Dhumal wore maroon-banded caps; Virbhadra Singh served six terms as Chief Minister, and Dhumal served two. Local music and dance are integral to cultural expression, especially during festivals and religious occasions. National and regional fairs, including temple fairs, occur in nearly every region, with Kullu Dussehra, Minjar mela, and Mahashivratri Mandi being nationally recognized. The local cuisine resembles northern Indian food with Punjabi and Tibetan influences, centered on lentils (Dāl), rice (chāwal or bhāț), vegetables (sabzī), and chapati, with non-vegetarian food more accepted due to limited fresh vegetables in hilly areas. Specialties include Siddu, Babru, Khatta, Mhanee, Channa Madra, Patrode, Mah ki dal, Chamba-style fried fish, Kullu trout, Chha Gosht, Pahadi Chicken, Sepu Badi, Auriya Kaddu, Aloo palda, Pateer, Makki di roti, Sarson ka saag, Chamba Chukh (Chouck), Bhagjery, and Chutney of Til. At independence, the literacy rate was only 8%, one of the lowest in India, but by 2011 it had risen to 82.8%, making Himachal one of the most literate states. There are over 10,000 primary schools, 1,000 secondary schools, and more than 1,300 high schools. Himachal became the first Indian state to make elementary education compulsory and accessible to every child, and it stands out for overcoming gender bias in education, with a female literacy rate of around 76% and near-universal primary school enrollment for girls. While gender disparities exist at higher levels, the state significantly outperforms others in closing the gap, with Hamirpur District showing particularly high literacy. The state government has invested heavily in education, shifting from quantitative expansion during the first six five-year plans to qualitative improvement and modernization after the seventh plan. In 2001, over 1,000 teacher aids were appointed through the Vidya Upasak Yojna. The Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan promotes universal elementary education and community school management, while the Rashtriya Madhyamik Shiksha Abhiyan (launched in 2009) focuses on quality secondary education. The state’s education standards are high compared to other Indian states, with notable institutions including Baddi University of Emerging Sciences and Technologies, Indian Institute of Technology Mandi, Indian Institute of Management Sirmaur, Himachal Pradesh University in Shimla, Central University of Himachal Pradesh in Dharamsala, National Institute of Technology Hamirpur, Indian Institute of Information Technology Una, Alakh Prakash Goyal University, Maharaja Agrasen University, and Himachal Pradesh National Law University. Prominent medical institutes include Indira Gandhi Medical College and Hospital in Shimla, Dr. Rajendra Prasad Government Medical College in Kangra, Rajiv Gandhi Government Post Graduate Ayurvedic College in Paprola, and Homoeopathic Medical College & Hospital in Kumarhatti, with a Government Dental College in Shimla being the state’s first recognized dental institute. The state government plans to establish three major nursing colleges to strengthen healthcare. CSK Himachal Pradesh Krishi Vishwavidyalya Palampur is a globally recognized hill agriculture institute, and Dr. Yashwant Singh Parmar University of Horticulture and Forestry is unique in India for its teaching, research, and extension in horticulture, forestry, and allied fields. Jawaharlal Nehru Government Engineering College was inaugurated in 2006 at Sundernagar. The National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) also operates a campus in Kangra.
